summary: This note collects excerpts on Santa Monica, California, covering early Asian American communities, the Tongva origins and competing accounts of the city's naming, its bicycle infrastructure, and the Douglas Aircraft Company's role in the 1924 round-the-world flight from Clover Field.
one_line: Excerpts on Santa Monica's history, Tongva roots, naming origins, bicycle programs, and Douglas Aircraft's 1924 world flight.
key_facts: Around the start of the 20th century, a growing population of Asian Americans lived in or near Santa Monica and Venice, including a Japanese fishing village near the Long Wharf.
White Americans were often well-disposed towards the Japanese but condescending towards the Chinese.
Japanese village fishermen were an integral economic part of the Santa Monica Bay community.
Santa Monica was long inhabited by the Tongva people, who called it Kecheek.
The party of explorer Gaspar de Portolà camped near Barrington and Ohio Avenues on August 3, 1769, the first non-indigenous group in the area.
One naming version honors the feast day of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, but her feast day is actually May 4.
Another version says Juan Crespí named it for the Kuruvungna Springs (Serra Springs), reminiscent of the tears Saint Monica shed over her son's early impiety.
Santa Monica launched a bicycle sharing system in November 2015 and is traversed by the Marvin Braude Bike Trail.
The League of American Bicyclists gave Santa Monica the Bicycle Friendly Community Award: Bronze in 2009 and Silver in 2013.
Santa Monica Spoke is a local chapter of the Los Angeles County Bicycle Coalition.
Donald Wills Douglas, Sr. built a plant in 1922 at Clover Field (Santa Monica Airport) for the Douglas Aircraft Company.

In 1924, four Douglas-built planes left Clover Field to attempt the first aerial circumnavigation; two returned after covering 27,553 miles (44,342 km) in 175 days, greeted September 23, 1924 by about 200,000 people.
The Douglas Company (later McDonnell Douglas) kept facilities in the city until the 1960s.
